result: The study measured the thickness of CA1 layers and their relative contributions to total CA1 thickness. The total CA1 thickness was 2.70 ± 0.62 mm, with SP contributing 42%, SLM 23%, SR 20%, alveus 13%, and SO 2%.
evaluation: Claims C26-C36 provide consistent quantitative measurements of layer thickness with standard deviations. The measurements are internally consistent (individual layer thicknesses sum appropriately to total thickness) and the relative percentages are correctly calculated from the absolute measurements. The methodology for obtaining these measurements is described in the methods section.

result: Volume fraction analysis revealed that neuropil constitutes >90% of all CA1 layers, with blood vessels occupying 4.79-7.58%, and neuronal cell bodies occupying 4.23% in SP but <2% in other layers. Significant differences were found between layers.
evaluation: Claims C37-C43 present volume fraction data with appropriate statistical testing (ANOVA with specific p-values). The methodology using the Cavalieri principle is well-established and properly described. The findings are supported by figures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and supplementary data. The statistical comparisons are appropriate for the data type.

result: A total of 24,752 synapses were reconstructed, with 19,269 included in final analysis after applying unbiased counting frames. Mean synaptic density was 0.67 ± 0.21 synapses/µm³, with sSP showing the highest density (0.99 ± 0.18) and SO the lowest (0.45 ± 0.19). Significant differences were found between sSP and both SO and SLM.
evaluation: Claims C4, C44-C49 provide the core quantitative findings on synaptic density with appropriate statistical testing (ANOVA). The large sample size (24,752 synapses) provides statistical power. The methodology includes proper corrections for tissue shrinkage and fixation artifacts. Statistical significance is appropriately reported with specific p-values. The data are supported by figures and tables.

result: Synapses exhibited random spatial distribution in all layers based on spatial point pattern analysis. Intersynaptic distance showed significant differences only between sSP (604.00 ± 38.08 nm) and SO (742.81 ± 63.06 nm), with strong inverse correlation (R² = 0.90) between synaptic density and intersynaptic distance.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by appropriate spatial statistical methods (F, G, K functions with CSR model comparison). The methodology is properly cited and the envelope approach with 99 simulations is standard. The correlation analysis (R² = 0.90) is strong and biologically meaningful. Results are supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

result: Most synapses in CA1 were excitatory (AS), with AS:SS ratios of approximately 95:5 in most layers, except SLM which showed 90:10. Significant differences were found between layers, with dSP showing lower AS frequency than sSP and SR, and SLM showing the highest proportion of SS (10.76%).
evaluation: Claims C5, C55-C62 present synapse type classification with appropriate statistical testing (χ² tests with specific p-values). The classification methodology based on PSD thickness is well-established (C55-C56 cite Ascoli et al., 2008). The large sample size provides adequate power for detecting differences. Results are supported by figures and consistent with established knowledge about excitatory/inhibitory synapse distributions.

result: Most synapses targeted dendritic spines (79.10%), particularly spine heads. Axospinous AS were the most abundant synapse type (78.04%), followed by axodendritic AS (11.44%). Significant layer-specific differences were observed, with SLM showing higher proportions of axodendritic synapses and sSP showing the highest proportion of axospinous AS.
evaluation: Claims C6, C63-C77 provide detailed postsynaptic target analysis with appropriate statistical testing (χ² tests). The methodology for identifying postsynaptic targets through serial section navigation is sound. The large sample size and multiple statistical comparisons are appropriately handled. Results are supported by multiple figures (Figures 4, 5) and supplementary data. The findings are consistent with known synaptic organization principles.

result: AS showed strong preference for dendritic spines (87.22%), almost exclusively on spine heads (>99.5%), while SS preferred dendritic shafts (89.93%). These preferences were statistically significant in all layers, with layer-specific variations in shaft type preferences (spiny vs. aspiny).
evaluation: Claims C78-C91 present postsynaptic preference analysis with consistent statistical testing (χ² tests, p<0.0001). The findings align with established principles of synaptic organization (excitatory synapses on spines, inhibitory on shafts). The detailed breakdown by spine location and shaft type provides novel quantitative data. Results are well-supported by figures and supplementary data.

result: Most synapses displayed macular shape (85.95% of AS, 80.55% of SS), followed by perforated (8.13% AS) and horseshoe-shaped (11.94% SS). Complex-shaped AS were more abundant in SLM, particularly horseshoe-shaped AS which were mainly located on dendritic shafts. Horseshoe-shaped synapses were significantly more abundant in SS than AS populations.
evaluation: Claims C7, C95-C104 provide comprehensive synaptic shape analysis with appropriate statistical testing (χ² tests). The classification system (macular, horseshoe, perforated, fragmented) is standard in the field. Layer-specific differences are well-documented with specific p-values. Results are supported by figures (Figure 2d-f, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and supplementary data. The findings are consistent with previous literature cited.

result: Dendritic spines receiving multiple synapses were found in all layers (2.11% of total spines), while single axospinous SS were extremely rare. Multiple-headed dendritic spines were observed (1.39% of total spines).
evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe relatively rare synaptic configurations with appropriate quantification. The percentages are clearly stated and supported by figures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c) and supplementary data. While these are minor findings in terms of frequency, they are accurately reported and contribute to the comprehensive characterization of CA1 synaptic organization.

result: Mean SAS area was 89,727.65 nm² for AS and 67,236.17 nm² for SS, with corresponding perimeters of 1,458.82 nm and 1,378.38 nm. No significant differences were found between layers for either synapse type, but AS had significantly larger areas than SS overall, with this difference significant only in dSP, sSP, and SLM when examined by layer. Strong correlation (R² = 0.81) was found between area and perimeter.
evaluation: Claims C105-C113 present synaptic size measurements with appropriate statistical testing (ANOVA, Mann-Whitney). The methodology using SAS extraction is well-described and validated. The correlation analysis is appropriate. However, the lack of layer differences (C109-C110) followed by specific layer differences (C112) requires careful interpretation - this appears to reflect overall ANOVA vs. post-hoc pairwise comparisons, which is statistically sound. Results are supported by figures and tables.

result: Frequency distributions of SAS areas showed similar shapes for AS and SS with positive skewness, with distributions greatly overlapping between synapse types and layers. Both AS and SS size distributions could be fitted to log-normal or log-logistic probability density functions.
evaluation: Claims C114-C116 describe the statistical distribution of synaptic sizes with appropriate testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov). The fitting to log-normal/log-logistic distributions is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and supplementary data showing distribution parameters. This type of analysis is standard for synaptic size data and the methodology is sound. The biological interpretation is discussed in relation to previous literature.

result: Axodendritic synapses tended to be larger than axospinous synapses, but this difference was only statistically significant in SLM for both AS (area and perimeter) and SS (area only).
evaluation: Claims C117-C120 present size analysis by postsynaptic target with appropriate statistical testing (Mann-Whitney). The finding that differences are significant only in SLM is interesting and biologically relevant. The statistical approach is appropriate for comparing two groups. Results are supported by Figure 6c-d and supplementary data.

result: Macular synapses were smaller than complex-shaped synapses for both AS and SS, but this difference was statistically significant only for AS (both area and perimeter).
evaluation: Claims C121-C122 present size analysis by synaptic shape with appropriate statistical testing (ANOVA). The finding that macular synapses are smaller is consistent with established knowledge about synaptic structure-function relationships. The lack of significance for SS may reflect smaller sample sizes for complex-shaped SS. Results are supported by Figure 6e-f and supplementary data.

result: Curvature measurements showed very little association with area (R² = 0.05) or perimeter (R² = 0.08). No differences in curvature were observed between AS and SS or between layers. Frequency distributions showed positive skewness with prevalence of flatter synapses. Fragmented synapses were more curved than macular synapses, with some layer-specific differences in curvature for specific shapes.
evaluation: Claims C123-C132 present curvature analysis with appropriate statistical testing and correlation analysis. The low correlation between curvature and size parameters (R² = 0.05-0.08) is an important finding showing these are independent measures. The statistical testing (ANOVA, Mann-Whitney) is appropriate. Results are supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and supplementary data. The finding that curvature is independent of size is novel and well-supported.

result: Interindividual variability was observed across multiple parameters and layers, but differences between cases were not consistent in terms of parameter, layer, or direction of change.
evaluation: Claims C133-C134 acknowledge interindividual variability with appropriate statistical documentation in supplementary files. The statement that differences were not consistent across parameters/layers/directions is important for interpretation. This honest reporting of variability strengthens the overall findings by showing which results are robust across individuals. The sample size (n=5 subjects) is appropriate for human autopsy studies but limits power for detecting consistent individual differences.

result: The neuropil represents the main structural component of CA1 (>90% of all layers), and SP contributes almost half of the total CA1 thickness (1.13 mm of 2.70 mm total).
evaluation: Claims C135-C136 summarize key structural findings from the volume fraction and thickness analyses. These are supported by the detailed measurements in C26-C43. The findings are biologically significant as they highlight major differences between human and rodent CA1 organization, which is discussed extensively in the manuscript.

result: Important anatomical differences exist between human and rodent hippocampus. In humans, SP can be up to 30 cell somata thick with wider neuronal separation, compared to ~5 cell bodies thick in rats. Human pyramidal cell basal and apical dendrites are intermixed in SP, while in rodents they are separated into SO and SR respectively.
evaluation: Claims C137-C141 compare human and rodent CA1 anatomy with appropriate citations. The findings about human SP thickness and dendritic organization are supported by the current data and previous work (Benavides-Piccione et al., 2020). The comparison to rodent anatomy is well-established in the literature. This represents an important contribution to understanding species differences in hippocampal organization.

result: Synaptic density in human CA1 (0.67 synapses/µm³) is much lower than in rodent CA1 (2.36-2.53 synapses/µm³ in mouse, 2.52 synapses/µm³ in rat). These differences, along with other anatomical and molecular differences, indicate remarkable differences between human and rodent CA1 that must be considered in translational studies.
evaluation: Claims C142-C147 make important comparative statements supported by current data and properly cited previous work from the same laboratory using identical methodology (FIB/SEM). The comparison is valid because the same techniques were used. The conclusion about translational implications (C147) is a reasonable inference from the data. This represents a major finding with significant implications for the field.

result: The synaptic characteristics observed in human CA1 (random distribution, high excitatory:inhibitory ratio, preference for spines, predominance of macular shape) are consistent with findings in other cortical regions and species, suggesting these are widespread organizational principles, though with regional variations in specific percentages.
evaluation: Claims C148-C155 place the current findings in context of previous literature with appropriate citations. The comparisons are valid and the conclusion about widespread organizational principles is reasonable. The acknowledgment of regional variations (e.g., C154 showing different percentages in transentorhinal cortex) demonstrates appropriate nuance. These comparisons strengthen the interpretation of the current findings.

result: Synaptic shape and size correlate with functional properties (release probability, strength, efficacy, plasticity). Complex-shaped synapses are larger than macular ones, and perforated synapses have more AMPA/NMDA receptors and are thought to have more long-lasting memory-related functionality.
evaluation: Claims C156-C159 connect structural findings to functional implications with appropriate citations. C156 cites multiple studies establishing structure-function relationships. C157 is supported by the current data (C121-C122). C158-C159 cite established literature about perforated synapses. However, C159 includes speculative language ("thought to constitute") which is appropriately cautious. The functional interpretations are reasonable but should be considered hypotheses requiring direct functional validation.

result: Synaptic size distributions fit log-normal or log-logistic functions, similar to distributions of other synaptic parameters (strength, EPSP size) and previous findings in rat cortex. The mechanisms generating size diversity may involve both activity-dependent and activity-independent processes, though whether quantization occurs in human hippocampus remains unclear.
evaluation: Claims C160-C166 discuss the statistical properties of size distributions with appropriate citations and comparisons to previous work. C160-C161 are supported by current data and previous work from the same lab. C162-C164 cite relevant literature making appropriate comparisons. C165 appropriately acknowledges a limitation (axons not traced). C166 cites recent work on mechanisms. The discussion is appropriately cautious about mechanistic interpretations while making valid statistical observations.

result: Excitatory synapses were larger than inhibitory ones overall, consistent with human transentorhinal cortex but contrasting with rat somatosensory cortex and CA1. Axodendritic synapses tended to be larger than axospinous synapses, with this difference significant in SLM. These findings agree with rat hippocampus data showing larger, more frequently perforated synapses on SLM dendrites.
evaluation: Claims C167-C173 make appropriate comparisons to previous literature with proper citations. The finding of species differences (C167-C168) is important and well-documented. The SLM-specific findings (C169-C173) are supported by current data and consistent with rat studies, suggesting conserved organizational principles despite overall species differences. The comparisons are valid and strengthen the interpretation.

result: Layer-specific differences in synaptic organization, particularly in SLM, may relate to the variety of inputs to these layers. SLM receives direct inputs from EC layer III/V, while other layers receive indirect inputs via DG and CA3. SLM also receives more inputs from amygdala, parietal/temporal cortex, and modulatory inputs from raphe nuclei and tegmental nucleus.
evaluation: Claims C174-C182 attempt to relate structural findings to connectivity patterns. However, C175 explicitly states that "detailed hippocampal human connectivity is far from being known" and most data are inferred from rodents/primates. While the connectivity patterns cited (C176-C182) are from established literature, the direct connection to the observed synaptic differences (C174, C180) is speculative. The interpretation is reasonable but represents a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated causal relationship. Direct connectivity studies in the same human tissue would be needed to definitively support these claims.

result: The CA3-CA1 connection is important for learning-induced potentiation, while EC-SLM projections modulate hippocampal information flow. High-frequency SLM stimulation evokes strong inhibition preventing CA1 pyramidal cell spiking, which could be supported by the elevated inhibitory synapse ratio in SLM. EC afferents contact both pyramidal cells and interneurons (including neurogliaform cells) in SLM, though whether the higher proportion of axodendritic synapses relates to specific interneuron circuit organization remains unclear.
evaluation: Claims C183-C189 attempt to connect structural findings to functional properties. C183-C185 cite established functional studies. C186 attempts to link current structural findings (elevated SS ratio in SLM) to previous functional observations, but this is correlative rather than causal. C187-C188 cite established connectivity patterns. C189 appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about the relationship between structural findings and circuit organization. While the functional context is valuable, the direct connections between structure and function remain speculative and would require combined structural-functional studies to confirm.

result: The study addresses a significant gap in knowledge about human hippocampal synaptic organization. While extensive data exists for animal models, very little information is available for human hippocampus, raising questions about extrapolation from animal models. Previous human studies used surgical specimens from patients with pathology, which cannot be considered representative of normal brain.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C20 establish the rationale and context for the study with appropriate citations. The gap in knowledge (C2, C13) is well-documented. The limitations of surgical specimens (C15-C17) are appropriately acknowledged. The importance of studying normal human brain (C18) is well-justified. These claims effectively establish the significance of the study and are supported by the literature.

result: FIB/SEM can be successfully applied to study synaptic organization in human autopsy brain tissue. The current study used this technology to perform comprehensive 3D analysis of synaptic organization across all CA1 layers from five human brain autopsies with short postmortem delays, examining multiple structural parameters. This represents the first extensive description of human hippocampal CA1 synaptic organization.
evaluation: Claims C3, C21-C25 describe the methodological approach and novelty of the study. C3 and C21 reference previous work by the authors demonstrating FIB/SEM feasibility. C22-C23 accurately describe the current study design. C24 claims this is the "first extensive description," which appears justified given the comprehensive nature of the analysis and the lack of comparable previous studies cited. C25 appropriately frames the significance. The methodology is well-validated and the novelty claim is supported.

result: Human brain tissue was obtained from five subjects with no recorded neurological/psychiatric alterations, with short postmortem delays (<4.5 hours). Tissue was analyzed for Braak stage and CERAD diagnosis (assigned zero score), though case AB1 showed sparse tau-immunoreactive cells and case AB4 showed amyloid plaques in subicular/parahippocampal regions.
evaluation: Claims C190-C193 describe the sample characteristics with appropriate detail. The short postmortem delays and lack of recorded pathology support the "normal" designation. However, C192-C193 reveal some pathological features in 2/5 cases, which somewhat complicates the "normal" characterization. The authors are transparent about these findings, which is appropriate. The Braak/CERAD scoring provides objective neuropathological assessment. While not perfectly "normal," these samples represent the best available human tissue for such studies.

result: The FIB/SEM methodology used specific imaging parameters (7-nA then 700-pA ion beam, 20-nm z-axis resolution, 5-nm/pixel xy resolution, 2048×1536 pixel images) to acquire 75 stacks totaling 29,322 µm³. Tissue shrinkage corrections were applied (area factor 0.933, linear factor 0.966, z-axis factor 0.901).
evaluation: Claims C194-C204 provide detailed methodological information about the FIB/SEM acquisition and corrections. The parameters are clearly specified and appropriate for the application. The shrinkage correction methodology is well-established and properly described. The total volume analyzed (29,322 µm³) is substantial. The methodology is reproducible based on the information provided. These technical details are essential for evaluating data quality and reproducibility.

result: This study constitutes the first extensive description of synaptic organization in the human hippocampal CA1 neuropil, revealing remarkable differences between layers, particularly in SLM compared to other layers.
evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C24 assert the novelty and significance of the study. The claim of being "first extensive description" appears justified given: (1) the comprehensive nature of the analysis (24,752 synapses, multiple parameters, all layers), (2) the use of normal autopsy tissue rather than surgical specimens, (3) the lack of comparable previous studies in the literature review, and (4) the 3D EM approach providing unprecedented detail. The finding of layer differences, particularly in SLM, is well-supported by the data and represents a major contribution.
